genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a woman recounts the path that led her to painting restoration
her interest begins while she cleans the workshop of a family member
at first she watched the cleaning of yellowed layers
little by little she is allowed to work on parts of a painting
she sets up her own premises in a courtyard after her training
her equipment includes a magnifying instrument and colors kept in jars
she has treated a pierced family painting and a wall painting faded by water
she can spend several weeks on a very small surface
she says she struggles to consider a job finished
she teaches two beginners that the work must be imperceptible
text: It started with a broom. As a girl she swept out her uncle's workshop, where damaged canvases came in to be saved, and she stayed on to watch. A swab of damp cotton would travel across a yellowed varnish, and the dullness simply lifted, which struck her as a kind of witchcraft. By her teens she was asking to hold a brush. They gave her frames first, then a corner of sky, then a face. Once her training was over she rented a tiny room at the back of a courtyard, with a swing-arm magnifier and pigments in glass jars. Work trickled in: a family portrait with a hole punched through it, a stairwell mural gone gray where damp had climbed the wall. One painted palm can keep her busy for weeks, she says, and the hard part is stopping. Two apprentices work beside her now, and she keeps telling them that good retouching is never seen.

units: the performance ends with a lukewarm reception from the audience
the staging comes down to a dark rug and two seats
no painted element appears on the stage
the lack of scenery leaves the audience without indications of where the action takes place
the text does not make up for this missing information
the musical accompaniment is played on the spot, hidden by a hanging
the sound covers the lines spoken faintly
one sequence carried by an actress is judged successful
the reviewer blames the failure on excessive austerity
text: The audience filed out with only scattered applause, and the coldness is easy to account for. Everything rests on a bare stage: a dark rug, two stools, not a single painted flat. Stripping it down might have thrown the focus onto the performers. It does the opposite, because nothing up there tells you where any of this is happening. So you start hunting the dialogue for clues, the dialogue withholds them, and the plot slides out of reach. The music, played live behind a hanging curtain, makes matters worse: it swallows the quieter lines, and whole speeches disappear under it. One passage deserves rescuing, a woman playing a scene of grief almost without moving, where the emptiness of the stage finally earns its keep. The evening fails through too much austerity, not through any shortage of ambition.

units: the writer is writing from a workshop where wood is worked
a piano had been damaged by water
the keys were sticking and the sound was altered
a specialist had judged tuning impossible in that state
the writer considered getting rid of the instrument
a neighbor who works with wood offers to take it apart and dry it
the padding spoiled by damp is replaced
the repair took the two people a whole cold season
the instrument now holds its tuning
the writer invites the reader to come and play it
text: I am writing from the joinery shop, wedged between two planks and the smell of warm glue. Do you remember the old piano I told you about, the one the rain got into? I had given it up for lost. The keys were sticking, the strings gave back a cracked note, and the man who came to look at it said there was no tuning an instrument in that state. I nearly let it go for firewood. Then a neighbor who works in wood offered another road: take the soundboard apart, dry the pieces flat under clamps, replace the felts the damp had eaten. The two of us spent a whole winter on it, with no plan worth the name. Since the day before yesterday it holds its tuning. I sit down in the evening and improvise clumsy things that nobody else will ever hear. Come and try it whenever you like; it is waiting for you.

units: the text contrasts sculpture obtained by removing material with sculpture obtained by pouring
carving does not allow what has been taken away to be put back
the pouring process starts from a clay model
a hollow impression is drawn from this model
metal or plaster is then poured into it
a cast piece can be reproduced as long as the model survives
the carver must examine the structure and the flaws of the block before starting
the caster must watch the tightness of the mold and the speed of setting
the carved surface keeps the mark of the tools
a cast piece shows lines where the parts of the mold joined
text: What separates a carved sculpture from a cast one? In the first, the maker takes material away and can never put it back, so every stroke of the chisel is final. In the second, he shapes a model in clay, pulls a hollow mold from it, then pours in metal or plaster: the form can be run again for as long as the model survives. Do the two ask for the same preparation? They do not. Carving demands that you read the block first, its grain and its hidden cracks, or it will split under the tool. Casting moves the trouble onto a tight mold and onto a cooling rate you have to master. And does the result look different? It does. Cut stone keeps the tracks of the tool, while a cast piece carries thin ridges where the parts of the mold met. What you pick follows from the effect you are after.

units: a museum official explains to visitors how a collection is formed
purchases follow the logic of completing an existing body of work
gifts raise the difficulty of the conditions set by the donor
some works are lent by another institution for a limited period
a visitor asks what becomes of the pieces that are never shown
the objects not on display are kept in crates with controlled air
these pieces remain available for research work
a student asks what share of the collection can be seen
the official admits that the share on show is small
text: Standing before the central case, the curator set out for his listeners how a collection comes together. He began with purchases: an institution rarely buys at random, and each piece that comes in has to round out a body of work already assembled. He turned to gifts, which raise a delicate matter, since a donor commonly expects the bequest to stay on permanent view. He mentioned loans as well, entrusted by another institution for a fixed term. A visitor asked what becomes of the pieces that are never shown. They sleep in storage, the curator answered, in crates with the air held steady, and researchers go on working with them. A student wanted to know how much of the holdings can be seen. The curator granted that the share is small, and that no room, however vast, could reveal it all at once.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first tapestries answered practical needs of insulation and division
they also served to signal status
the earliest patterns were geometric and repetitive
specialist workshops appear near noble courts
the hangings then begin to tell stories in pictures
the figures were known by the objects that went with them
dyeing improves and offers brighter colors
the trade in these cloths enriches merchant towns
a model painted by an artist was reproduced by anonymous workers
mechanization reduced this craft to a narrow luxury market
text: The earliest figured weavings answered needs that were wholly practical: to line a cold wall, to shut one room off from another, to mark a rank. The patterns of those first hangings were geometric, easy to repeat and easy to keep in the memory. Specialist workshops then grew up around the noble courts, and the hanging turned into a story, whole scenes read from left to right, each figure known by the object that went with it. Demand pushed the dyers to widen their range, and the glowing threads drawn from insects and from roots made the fortune of several trading towns. After that came the painted cartoon, laid out by an artist and then followed stitch by stitch by weavers who never signed their work. The mechanical loom cut this painstaking craft down at last to a narrow luxury trade.

units: the text explains the darkening of old paintings
the protective layer laid on the surface breaks down on contact with air
this layer takes on a yellow tint that changes all the colors
the resistance of coloring matter varies with its origin
coloring matter of plant origin fades under too strong a light
the loss of one color can change the tint of a whole area
deposits from burning form a greasy film on the work
what is visible today differs from the original appearance
careful cleaning is justified by these changes
text: You have surely stood in front of an old painting at some point and wondered where that brownish haze over it comes from. Blame the varnish first. A coat of it goes on to protect the surface, but the film oxidizes with the air, it turns yellow, and in the end it tints the whole picture the way dirty glass would. Then there are the pigments themselves. Some colors hold for generations; others, drawn from plants, fade as soon as they take too much light, so a blue sky can drift toward green once the yellow that warmed it has gone. Add the smoke of lamps and hearths, which leaves a greasy skin over everything. The upshot is that the painting in front of you barely keeps the color it had on the day it left the workshop. That is exactly why a careful cleaning is worth the trouble.

units: a water leak flooded the dressing room the night before the first performance
the costumes ended up soaked
the colors of a thick fabric bled onto light-colored clothes
giving up the performance would have meant a financial loss
playing in rehearsal clothes was judged unacceptable
the technical manager suggests deliberately unifying the spoiled tints
all the cloths are dipped again in a single pale bath
the lighting is changed to match these new shades
the audience knew nothing of the accident and enjoyed the result
the company has kept this version born of a mishap
text: On the night before the opening, a pipe burst backstage, and the company found the dressing room under water, costumes lying in soaked heaps on the tiles. The velvet of the coats had bled onto the pale shirts, and the stiffened collars hung limp. Calling it off would cost a fortune; going on in rehearsal clothes felt beneath them. The stage manager offered a way out nobody expected: since the dyes had run anyway, why not let the whole stage look washed out on purpose? The team spent the night dipping every piece of cloth in one pale bath until the range settled into an even pinkish gray. The lighting crew cooled their lamps to match. The audience, knowing nothing of the flood, praised a look both bold and coherent. The company has kept that accidental version ever since.

units: the text sets out two printmaking techniques to choose between
the first consists in cutting into a metal support
the metal is covered with a protective film before the drawing
a corrosive liquid deepens the lines opened with a point
the second technique calls for clearing from a block of wood the parts meant to stay white
this second method allows no correction
both processes involve inking and then wiping the surface
the paper used must be dampened before it goes under the press
the sunken process gives a thick line that can be felt with a finger
the wood process gives flat areas with clean edges
text: Choose your road before anything else, for two hands are open to you and they do not ask for the same kind of patience. To cut into metal, take a plate coated with a thin varnish, draw your design on it with a needle, then lower the plate into a biting bath: the acid deepens the lines you have opened. To cut in relief, take a block of soft wood and clear away instead everything that must stay white; here nothing at all can be taken back. Either way, ink the surface, wipe it clean, lay down a sheet of damp paper and roll the whole thing under the press. The eye tells the two apart: the sunken line holds a heavy charge and stands up under the finger, while the wood gives flat fields and clean edges. Pull one sheet, look hard at it, correct what needs correcting, and begin again.

units: a center for conserving recordings has opened in a converted industrial building
a first bench deals with magnetic tape
these tapes go through an oven before they are played
this heating stops the recording layer from sticking
a second bench reads discs with a contactless optical device
a third service writes the description of the sound documents
this description calls for listening to each recording in full
the backup copies are spread over two sites
the head of the center holds the documentation to matter more than the carrier itself
a recording without a description can no longer be found
text: A center for sound conservation has just opened in a converted industrial hall, and the man who runs it walked us through the work bench by bench. The first bench handles magnetic tape: the reels go into an oven before playback, so that the recording layer stops clinging to itself. The second reads cut discs, whose grooves an optical sensor traces without ever touching them. A third service writes the description of each recording, slow work, since indexing means listening to every piece from end to end. A separate room holds the backup copies, kept in two different buildings. The man who runs it presses one point above all: the carrier matters less than the description filed with it, because a recording nobody has described cannot be found again and has all but stopped existing.
